TM Krishna: For generations, ‘Hum Dekhenge’ has stripped the cloak off powerful narcissists Maharashtra’s recognition of women farmers will break gender barriers CEC protest: Mamata Banerjee, Arvind Kejriwal among Opposition leaders detained ‘A focus on literature that is part of everyday life’: Onaiza Drabu on editing a Kashmiri anthology Sunday book pick: A tale of a resentful housewife in Shashi Deshpande’s novel ‘That Long Silence’ Wave of protests shows that Indian democracy’s greatest strength is its ‘million mutinies’ “I wanted to make the case for the fact that literature is everywhere; it is omnipresent.” That is what Onaiza Drabu aimed to do with The Big Book of Kashmiri Literature , the anthology she has edited that illustrates the richness of Kashmiri literature, land, and people through a diverse canon of expressions. The anthology brings together the works of several historical saints, scholars, unlettered poets, and voices of Kashmir, ranging from the fourteenth century to the contemporary era. In a conversation with Scroll, Drabu spoke about the making of The Big Book of Kashmiri Literature , the inspiration for the project, the process of collecting literary works from earlier centuries and selecting texts for an anthology of this scale. How did you get the idea to compile The Big Book of Kashmiri Literature ? I started my journey into exploring Kashmiri language and literature way back in 2013. That is when I started drawing the earliest illustrations of proverbs for something called Lipton Chai Blog . In fact, Scroll was the first platform to feature some of these. Those were the early days of memes and they got very popular. It was then that I started reading Kashmiri literature in translation and a few years later, started working on my first book on Kashmiri folklore. Starting then, I began reading a lot more. I could not read and write in Kashmiri, as during my time in school there was no Kashmiri in the curriculum, so it took me a bit of effort to learn the script and get quick at reading. When the publisher came with a suggestion to compile The Big Book of Kashmiri Literature, I was already thinking about Kashmiri-to-English translation. I had worked on an essay for a book titled Violent Phenomenon , which collected essays around the topic of decolonising translation. I wrote about translation and the powers that determine what is translated, how it is translated and who gets published in the first place. It was a piece on the literary translation landscape in Kashmir, considering the various dynamics the language operates under – especially keeping the orality inherent in the language at its centre. I thought it was a serendipitous moment to actually define what a compilation, an ideal compilation, of Kashmiri literature could be. That is how I first drew up the table of contents of what would be the book. I had a few aims with this: I wanted to keep poetry and rhyme inherent in the language at the centre of it. I wanted all genres represented. I wanted a range of writers – those who publish within the traditional publishing ecosystem and outside of it. I also wanted a range of translators and translation styles – many of them for whom translation is beyond the remit of their daily work and profession. So it is an assemblage of translators, genres, types of writers, and styles of translation across a period of time. How did you collect these poems and literary works from the old centuries, and what difficulties did you face during the process? Were there particular sources or works that were especially difficult to trace or access? I think collecting the works was the easier part, but the labour involved in anthologising over these last few years was wider, especially with the range of writers and translators involved in the book – across geographies, time zones, and time periods. I started with reading literary histories, in Kashmiri, English, and Urdu. And then reading and mapping a whole range of literature in translation. From amongst what existed, I wrote to translators whose work spoke to me and then together we put together what they would like to translate or were working on already and how to bring it together. The attacks brought the number of Palestinians killed in Khan Yunis and Jabalia since early Sunday to four, including a child. In northern Gaza, seven-year-old Palestinian child Jihad Al-Ghandour died from wounds sustained when Israeli forces shot him near Al-Hawja Street in the Jabalia refugee camp . Local sources confirmed his death on Sunday, adding to the number of Palestinian children killed in attacks despite the ceasefire. Meanwhile, six Palestinians were wounded by Israeli gunfire in central, western, and southern Khan Yunis. Two others were injured when Israeli military vehicles opened fire toward tents sheltering displaced families near Shuja’iyya Junction, east of Gaza City. Read Also: Israel Records 11,620 Demolitions in West Bank and Jerusalem in Three Years In Gaza City, Israeli troops carried out demolition operations in the Shuja’iyya neighborhood in the east and the Al-Zeitoun neighborhood in the southeast, alongside continued gunfire and artillery shelling. In central Gaza, Israeli military vehicles opened fire east of the Al-Bureij refugee camp as illumination flares were launched over the area. Israeli artillery also targeted Rafah in southern Gaza. Meanwhile, Israeli military vehicles fired heavily toward tents housing displaced Palestinians in the Al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Yunis and Rafah. In its daily statistical report on Sunday, Gaza’s Ministry of Health announced that seven Palestinian victims had been brought to hospitals across the territory during the previous 24 hours. The casualties included six Palestinians newly killed and one who succumbed to earlier injuries. The ministry also recorded 28 injuries during the same period. According to the ministry, the number of Palestinians killed since the ceasefire began in October 2025 has risen to 1,488, while 5,281 others have been injured. Rescue and medical teams have also recovered the bodies of 836 Palestinians during the ceasefire period. Read Also: Hundreds Displaced as Israel Expands Control Over Gaza’s Shuja’iya The ministry reported that the cumulative Palestinian death toll from Israel’s war on Gaza since October 7, 2023, has reached 74,377 killed and 175,398 injured. Despite the truce, Israeli forces have continued to carry out airstrikes, artillery shelling, and gunfire across the Gaza Strip, resulting in further Palestinian casualties. The targeting of tents sheltering displaced families, residential neighborhoods, and civilians has drawn concern from human rights organizations, which have called for accountability and full implementation of the ceasefire. The Israeli military maintains that its operations are defensive responses to threats from militant groups, while Palestinian sources and international observers have described the continuing attacks as aggression against civilians and infrastructure. The ongoing violence underscores the fragility of the truce and the need for diplomatic efforts to prevent further loss of life. Gaza’s humanitarian situation remains dire, with medical facilities facing shortages of fuel and medicine, the agricultural sector nearing collapse, and thousands of families living in damaged buildings at risk of collapse. sources.evidenceText: BRUSSELS, Belgium: NATO’s top military commander is expected to deliver a warning to Russia on Monday over the alliance’s ability to counter any attack, as worries grow over the threat from Moscow. NATO officials have said US General Alexus Grynkewich — the alliance’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe — will elaborate his “theory of victory” over any potential attack at a security conference in Warsaw. The move from the top military commander comes as NATO seeks to send a message to Moscow to halt what Western officials say is a “hybrid” campaign of sabotage and interference against Ukraine’s backers in the war against Russia. Fears have grown in recent months that the Kremlin is stepping up its actions after high-profile incidents including the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at a German airport. “The Supreme Allied Commander Europe’s theory of victory is simple: maintain NATO’s advantage, which is consistent with and grounded upon the alliance’s deterrence and defense plans,” Col. Martin O’Donnell, a spokesman for the US general, said last week. “But given the unsettled and complex global security environment, we need to set conditions now to deter aggression and, if necessary, win if attacked,” O’Donnell said, noting the theory sets out a framework to do just that. NATO — which was founded in the wake of World War II to counter the Soviet Union — traditionally closely guards its defense plans to counter any attack by Russia. Grynkewich’s intervention looks unlikely to divulge many new details on NATO’s strategy and is intended to both send a signal to Moscow and reassure members on the alliance’s eastern flank. NATO insists it remains a defensive alliance and has no intention of attacking Russia. Western officials say that Moscow’s “hybrid attacks” have become more reckless as the Kremlin’s forces are stalled in Ukraine, and that they risk causing significant loss of life. The alliance — whose primary purpose is deterring an armed Russian invasion — has struggled to work out how to cope with incidents in the grey zone beneath open conflict. NATO civilian head Mark Rutte has urged countries to keep “calm, carry on and support Ukraine.” “We should not be naive... about Russia, but they know we are stronger,” Rutte said last month. But the uptick in Russian activity comes at a time of potential vulnerability for Europe. Allies are currently bracing for possible cuts to US forces in Europe as the Pentagon conducts a review of its deployments on the continent. The results of the process are expected to be announced toward the end of the year. European countries are already rushing to bolster their militaries as doubts have soared over the reliability of the United States under President Donald Trump. The attacks underscore how the conflict is increasingly affecting Saudi territory as Riyadh deepens its support for the Yemeni government’s military campaign. Pakistan has had a military presence in Saudi Arabia for decades, he said. Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi’s security was “absolute,” Chaudhry said. He described the alliance as a mechanism for collective defense under which an attack on one member would be considered an attack on all. But he would not be drawn on whether Pakistani troops would be involved in any operations across the border in Yemen. “Whenever there is a military conflict, no participating country starts disclosing how and where it is going to employ its forces,” he said, adding the any involvement would be “defensive in nature.” “The objective of this alliance is not to start labelling enemies, enemies, enemies, friends, friends, friends. sources.evidenceText: Bangladesh is confronting the world’s worst measles outbreak, with nearly 1,000 suspected and confirmed deaths reported since March as a collapse in vaccination coverage leaves hundreds of thousands of children vulnerable and hospitals struggling to cope with an unprecedented surge in patients. Bangladesh, once regarded as a country that had come close to eliminating measles, is facing an extraordinary public-health crisis, with 999 suspected and confirmed measles-related deaths reported since the outbreak intensified in March. More than 166,000 suspected measles cases have been recorded, including 19,835 laboratory-confirmed infections, according to Bangladesh Health Ministry data. More than 146,000 suspected patients have been hospitalised, placing severe pressure on already crowded medical facilities. The outbreak has spread across the country and is being described by international health authorities as the largest measles outbreak currently recorded anywhere in the world. The scale of the crisis marks a dramatic reversal for Bangladesh, which had previously maintained high measles vaccination coverage and made substantial progress toward elimination. Health experts say the outbreak is closely linked to gaps in routine childhood immunisation that emerged during years of disruption, including the COVID-19 pandemic and political turmoil in 2024 and 2025. Missed vaccinations left growing numbers of children without adequate protection against measles. Supply and procurement problems further complicated efforts to restore routine immunisation, allowing the number of susceptible children to increase. Infants are particularly vulnerable. Children younger than nine months are generally too young for routine measles vaccination, meaning that high levels of community immunity are crucial to protect them from exposure. The World Health Organization has stressed that measles is among the most contagious infectious diseases and that sustained high vaccination coverage is essential to prevent outbreaks. Two-dose vaccination is the foundation of measles prevention, while at least 95% coverage is generally needed to maintain population-level protection. Emergency vaccination campaign reaches millions Bangladesh launched an emergency measles-rubella vaccination campaign in April with support from the WHO, UNICEF and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance. The initial campaign began on April 5 in 30 high-risk subdistricts covering 18 districts before being expanded nationwide. The programme targeted children aged six months to five years, particularly those who had missed routine vaccinations. By May 10, more than 18 million children had been vaccinated, reaching nearly the entire national target of approximately 18.03 million children. The campaign also reached vulnerable children living in Rohingya refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar, where more than 166,000 children were vaccinated. But health experts warn that an emergency campaign alone cannot solve the underlying problem. The priority now is to identify children who have received no routine vaccinations, restore regular immunisation services and ensure that vaccine supplies remain reliable. WHO officials have described the campaign as an essential emergency response but stressed that sustained routine immunisation will be necessary to prevent another outbreak. The unprecedented number of infections has placed enormous pressure on Bangladesh’s healthcare system. Hospitals are struggling with overcrowded wards, shortages of beds and essential paediatric supplies while medical workers treat children suffering not only from measles but also from potentially severe complications such as pneumonia and neurological problems. The situation is particularly concerning because measles can weaken the immune system and leave children vulnerable to other infections. The health system is also facing another major challenge: a rapidly escalating dengue outbreak. As of early September, Bangladesh had recorded 42,590 dengue hospitalisations and 117 deaths in 2026. On one day alone, 1,558 people were admitted to hospitals and four deaths were reported, further intensifying pressure on medical facilities already dealing with the measles crisis. The simultaneous outbreaks of measles and dengue have created a severe test for hospitals, particularly in densely populated areas such as Dhaka. Health authorities and experts have pointed to immunisation disruptions that accumulated over several years, leaving pockets of children without adequate protection. WHO reporting during the early stages of the outbreak found that measles had spread to most of Bangladesh's districts, while health workers encountered families whose children had missed multiple routine vaccinations. In some communities, health teams identified so-called “zero-dose” children—youngsters who had never received routine childhood vaccines. Such discoveries have highlighted the extent of the immunity gaps behind the outbreak. The emergency campaign has therefore served not only as a response to the outbreak but also as an opportunity to identify children who have been missed by the country's routine immunisation system. Bangladesh's measles crisis is particularly striking because the country had previously achieved high vaccination coverage and made significant progress toward controlling the disease. WHO data showed only a few hundred confirmed measles cases annually in Bangladesh between 2021 and 2025. By April 2026, however, confirmed infections had already surged dramatically, demonstrating how quickly measles can return when immunity levels fall. The current outbreak is therefore being viewed as a warning for other countries that have made progress against vaccine-preventable diseases: elimination gains can be rapidly lost when routine immunisation systems are disrupted. sources.evidenceText: The long-awaited Eglinton Crosstown LRT is finally set to open its doors to passengers this Sunday, marking a significant milestone in Toronto's transit history. But the journey to this moment has been far from smooth sailing. The Controversial Opening: The Toronto Transit Commission (TTC) CEO, Mandeep Lali, has confirmed the opening, but it won't be the grand celebration some might expect. Unlike the Finch West LRT launch, there will be no ceremonial first ride. Instead, the Crosstown's debut will be low-key, cautious, and phased, reflecting the project's troubled past. Lali highlighted recent 'huge milestones' achieved by the TTC and Metrolinx, assuring the public that safety concerns have been addressed. However, just last week, he expressed worries about the light rail line's emergency brake systems, which had been activating randomly. After meeting with the line's designers and builders, Lali is now confident in the system's readiness. A Long Time Coming: The Eglinton Crosstown LRT has been a massive undertaking, with construction starting 15 years ago and an original opening date set for six years ago. The 19-kilometer line, with 25 stations, will connect Kennedy Station in east Toronto to Mount Dennis in the west. But the road to completion has been riddled with challenges. Challenges and Delays: The project faced significant delays, with the province stopping short of providing an opening date in 2023 due to the builder's lack of a credible timeline. The line also encountered legal battles and ongoing disputes between the contractor and Metrolinx, further complicating matters. These issues have led to a cost of over $13 billion, as reported by Metrolinx last fall. Phased Opening and Service Details: The LRT will begin service in phases, with trains running from 5:30 a.m. to 11 p.m. on weekdays and 7:30 a.m. to 11 p.m. on weekends. This cautious approach is understandable given the recent struggles with the Finch West LRT, which has suffered breakdowns and service interruptions. Controversial Opinions: Coun. Dianne Saxe has voiced skepticism, suggesting the line is opening prematurely. She believes it's a shame to open after 15 years when it's not fully ready. This sentiment is shared by some residents, who have endured years of construction-related congestion and business disruptions on Eglinton Avenue. Looking Ahead: As the LRT prepares to welcome its first passengers, the question remains: Will the Eglinton Crosstown LRT live up to the expectations of Torontonians? And what lessons can be learned from the challenges faced during its development? The public's feedback during this initial phase will be crucial in shaping the future of this ambitious transit project. What are your thoughts on the upcoming opening? sources.evidenceText: The Canada Voice network · 13 local news sites across Ontario Toronto City Council has signed off on an $18.9-billion operating budget and the largest 10-year capital plan in the city's history, including frozen TTC fares and a property tax increase below inflation. October 10, 2026 at 6:18 p.m. · Updated October 11, 2026 at 2:10 p.m. · 2 min read Toronto City Council has approved the city's 2026 budget, signing off on an $18.9-billion operating plan and a 10-year capital budget that the city says is the largest in its history. The budget — Mayor Olivia Chow's third since her election in 2023 — was passed at a special meeting of council on Tuesday, according to a statement from Councillor Paula Fletcher , who represents Toronto-Danforth and published a budget breakdown on her website. The centrepiece of the plan is a $63.1-billion capital budget and plan covering 2026 to 2035, which Fletcher described as the biggest 10-year capital commitment the city has ever made. Fletcher said the budget's affordability measures — including frozen TTC fares and free meals for students — would save a working family with two children about $1,200 a year on groceries and transportation costs alone. The property tax increase for 2026 is set at 2.2 per cent, which Fletcher noted is below the rate of inflation. The budget also proposes what she called a fairer approach to funding city services, asking "empty home speculators and luxury property buyers" — the top 2 per cent of all buyers — to contribute more. The budget also includes $788 million in new savings and efficiencies, according to Fletcher, who said the city's financial position has improved over the past two years under Chow's leadership. Among the service investments, the budget funds seven-day-a-week library access and increases funding for tenant supports, home upgrade grants, flood protection, and programs that help seniors stay in their homes. On public safety, Fletcher said shootings, youth violence and 911 wait times have all significantly decreased. The budget builds on that trend, she said, by investing in more firefighters, paramedics, police officers and mental health workers, while boosting crime prevention programs. More than 25,000 residents took part in budget consultations held in October 2025, including telephone town halls and local events such as Fletcher's own budget town hall, ensuring the final plan reflected residents' priorities, her statement said. "I was pleased to support Mayor Chow's budget and her progressive vision of a more affordable, caring and safe Toronto," Fletcher wrote in her post. The budget vote came during a busy final stretch of the 2022-2026 council term. According to Fletcher's update, councillors also dealt with a maximum heat bylaw to protect tenants during extreme heat, a new funding deal to build more housing, and the provincial upload of the Gardiner Expressway and Don Valley Parkway. Other items on the agenda included Fletcher's motion about odours from the Ashbridges Bay sewage treatment plant, a redevelopment plan for Ookwemin Minising, and increased support from the mayor's office for vulnerable youth and low-income tenants. The stated goal is a transport system with greater frequency, capacity and reliability. For commuters, the intended outcome is improved access to and from downtown Toronto and Hamilton — the two anchors of the GTHA region. The alliance contract model places ONxpress in a collaborative delivery structure with Metrolinx, sharing risk and decision-making across the execution phase rather than operating under a conventional fixed-price arrangement. Metrolinx and the Ontario government have framed GO Expansion as one of the country's most significant rail undertakings. The programme aims to transform what is largely a peak-hour commuter network into a more frequent, all-day service. For FCC, the contract marks a further step in its North American expansion, pairing with Aecon, one of Canada's largest construction firms. No specific value for the newly executed alliance contracts was disclosed in the announcement. Works are expected to progress under the alliance structure with Metrolinx in the coming years. sources.evidenceText: Vladimir Putin pledged to do "everything in our power" to help end the war between Iran and the US on Thursday, positioning Russia as a would-be Middle East mediator while continuing his own full-scale invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year.The Russian president made the remarks at a bilateral meeting with his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian in Avazeh, on Turkmenistan's Caspian coast, praising Tehran for making what he called "genuine efforts" to resolve the war.Pezeshkian said Iran and the US had exchanged proposals to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and that Tehran was reviewing and amending them before consolidating them through mediators. Despite ongoing US attacks, he said Iran would not leave the negotiating table."We are talking, but every time we negotiate with the United States, they attack again," Pezeshkian said. "Nevertheless, we will not abandon the negotiating table and dialogue."He said the revisions, once finalised, would be put to mediators. "We are supposed to sit down through the existing mediators and consolidate them," he said.It was the seventh meeting between the two presidents since Pezeshkian took office, following a phone call on 7 October — Putin's birthday — in which the pair discussed regional developments and the Iran-US negotiations.The two previously met in person on 1 September on the sidelines of the Shanghai Co-operation Organisation summit in Bishkek.Russia is not a mediator in the US-Iran negotiations. So far, Qatar and Pakistan have led the talks.Ties further deepenMilitary, diplomatic and economic relations between Iran and Russia have strengthened since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.The Iran war, which began with joint US-Israeli strikes on 28 February, has sparked more frequent consultations between Moscow and Tehran on political and material support and financial co-operation.Since 2022, Iran has supplied Russia with Shahed drone technology — which Moscow has since copied to create its own Geran-type variant, a key tool in its daily attacks on Ukrainian civilian and infrastructure targets — and short-range missiles.Moscow also faces accusations of providing Tehran with targeting information for attacks on US interests in the Middle East.Trade between the two countries rose by more than 21% in 2025 and continued on the same trajectory through the first seven months of 2026, Putin said, adding that relations were developing under a comprehensive strategic partnership agreement signed early last year.Pezeshkian described the current situation as an opportunity to deepen co-operation and said Tehran and Moscow should coordinate "with greater speed and strength."Billion-dollar loan delayedIranian state-run media reported in the days before the meeting that Russia was ready to extend a $1 billion loan to Tehran, described as the first tranche of a $20 billion package agreed at a meeting between Supreme National Security Council secretary Ali Larijani and Putin.The semi-official IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency said arrangements to disburse the sum were complete, but disagreements among Iranian authorities over how to spend the money prevented Tehran from providing the account number needed to complete the transfer.Iran's Planning and Budget Organisation wants to use the funds to import cars and collect customs duties, the Oil Ministry wants them for oil equipment, and the Agriculture Ministry is seeking to allocate them to basic commodity imports, according to the same report.The bilateral meeting took place on the eve of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) leaders' summit — a gathering of nine former Soviet republic heads focused on regional co-operation — and a separate Caspian Sea environmental conference, also held in Turkmenistan, bringing together the leaders of Iran, Russia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan.

sources.title: A Distant Planet Emitted a Burst of Radio Waves. Why? - Nautilus
sources.evidenceText: Astronomers pinpoint the origin of a 10 billion‑year‑old millisecond signal from space More than 10 billion years ago, something in a distant galaxy gave off an incredibly bright burst of radio waves which lasted just a few milliseconds. In new research published today in Science , our team tracked it back to its origin in a small galaxy filled with many young stars, when the universe was only one-fifth of its current age. Fast radio bursts like this one are a mystery scientists have been trying to unravel for almost 20 years since they were first discovered. Our discovery is the most distant such burst whose host galaxy has yet been identified. Finding a Radio Signal from 10 Billion Years Ago We detected the burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, with the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa, using a system called MeerTRAP which is designed to catch fast-changing transient radio signals from space in real time. The different frequencies of the radio burst arrived at slightly different times. We call this effect “dispersion”, and it happens because the signal has travelled through a lot of electrically charged material in space on its journey to Earth. By measuring the amount of dispersion, we can tell how much of this material the signal has passed through – which in turn lets us calculate how far the signal has travelled and how far away from us it was created. The FRB 20240304B burst showed a large amount of dispersion, which suggested it was probably coming from a great distance. We were also able to pinpoint its position on the sky. But when we looked at that position with large ground-based telescopes like the Keck Telescopes , we couldn’t see a host galaxy. The galaxy was simply too faint. So we turned to the James Webb Space Telescope ( JWST ). The space telescope’s infrared camera revealed a tiny galaxy very close to the position of the fast radio burst. We then broke down light from the galaxy into the spectrum of different frequencies that made it up. We know what part of this spectrum “should” look like, and seeing how those frequencies have changed lets us calculate how fast the galaxy is moving away from us due to the expansion of the universe – which in turn lets us figure out how old it is. These calculations confirmed that we were looking at a galaxy 10.6 billion years ago. It contains only about 10 million times the mass of our Sun, which is a tiny fraction of the mass of our own Milky Way galaxy. The host galaxy appears to be a young galaxy still forming many stars, with a very low amount of metal content, and very different from many of the larger galaxies in which most other fast radio bursts have been found. This is consistent with one theory about the source of at least some fast radio bursts – that they are produced by young, highly magnetised neutron stars called magnetars . At the same time, fast radio bursts come in different shapes and sizes, we don’t think all of them necessarily have the same kind of origin. However, observations like ours give us another piece of the puzzle. By studying the host galaxies and the environments of fast radio bursts across cosmic time, we can start to understand which types of galaxies and stellar environments produce them. The most exciting thing about this discovery, however, may not be the distance itself. As the radio signal made its way to Earth, it picked up the imprint of everything it passed through, bearing a record of the magnetic fields, changes in the space environment, and turbulence that it encountered. This makes it a gold mine of information about the cosmos that is otherwise difficult to access. This includes how electrons are distributed through the cosmic web, as well as information on magnetic fields that pervade the universe. As the signal encounters magnetic fields along the way they subtly twist the orientation of its radio waves. By measuring this twist, we learn about the magnetic field complexities across many billions of light years. FRB 20240304B does more than tell us about one distant galaxy. It gives us a new data point for studying how electrically charged matter has been distributed through the universe over cosmic time, and also how magnetised the cosmos is. Our discovery has shown for the first time that fast radio bursts were being produced all the way back to around 3 billion years after the Big Bang, during the period when the universe was most actively forming stars and galaxies. This lets us probe electrically charged matter across about 80% of cosmic history. Finding fast radio bursts at such large distances is difficult because of the combination of detecting increasingly faint bursts and identifying galaxies that are themselves extremely faint. With larger samples of distant fast radio bursts, we can use these brief flashes as cosmic signposts, revealing how matter is spread through the universe, how galaxies grow, and how the space between them changes over time. sources.evidenceText: Yu-Cheng Zhu, Jia-Xi Zeng and Xin-Zheng Li of Peking University report the discovery of a previously unknown lattice quantum disordered phase within superconductors. Their work reveals this phase occupies a triangular region in the P-T phase diagram, with its left boundary aligning precisely with the critical temperature where superconductivity begins on a material’s “left flank.” Identifying this alignment, the researchers establish lattice quantum disorder as a key component of the superconducting pairing mechanism and a unifying framework for both predicting new superconductors and understanding condensed matter physics more broadly. Prevailing models of superconductivity have long centered on electron behavior. But new calculations reveal a previously unrecognized lattice quantum disordered (LQD) phase that precisely defines the onset of superconductivity on one side of the material’s performance range. This phase, discovered through first-principles calculations incorporating nuclear quantum many-body effects, manifests as a triangular region within the pressure-temperature (P-T) phase diagram of certain superconductors. The discovery challenges conventional phonon theory, which traditionally omits the complex quantum interactions of atomic nuclei, leading to inaccurate structural phase diagrams and a flawed foundation for understanding superconductivity. Researchers found that the LQD phase arises from quantum fluctuations stabilizing a disordered state, resulting in lattice dynamics beyond the conventional description of atomic vibrations as simple phonons. This quantum disorder isn’t merely a side effect. The work demonstrates that the superconducting transition on the left flank of the dome originates from the structural transition into this LQD phase, suggesting a direct link between nuclear quantum effects and the emergence of superconductivity. The team employed path-integral molecular dynamics (PIMD) to rigorously account for these nuclear quantum many-body effects from first principles, a method that goes beyond standard molecular dynamics by treating nuclei as quantum objects rather than classical particles. This approach allowed for a more accurate determination of structural phase boundaries and the identification of the LQD phase itself. The researchers determined the true phase transition point by examining the curvature of the free energy surface, which fully accounts for both thermal and quantum effects, offering a broadly applicable criterion for structural instability. The newly identified LQD phase is delineated by a triangular region on the P-T phase diagram, bounded by a classical boundary determined via molecular dynamics and a quantum boundary calculated using PIMD. The intersection of these boundaries defines the temperature at which quantum effects are overwhelmed by thermal fluctuations. The impact of isotopic composition is also apparent. Deuterium, with its greater mass and weaker quantum effects, exhibits a higher-pressure quantum phase boundary and a lower temperature of approximately 160 Kelvin, compared to the 220 Kelvin observed for hydrogen. The alignment of the LQD phase’s left boundary with the superconducting dome’s left flank isn’t coincidental; the calculations show that as temperature increases, the boundary of the LQD phase shifts to higher pressure, mirroring the steepness of the superconducting dome. This correspondence strongly suggests a causal relationship, indicating that the transition into the LQD phase is fundamental to initiating superconductivity on that side of the dome. This new understanding could allow for the design of materials with enhanced superconducting properties and a deeper comprehension of the complex interplay between nuclear and electronic behavior in these materials. This finding challenges conventional models that prioritize electron behavior, instead highlighting the important role of the lattice structure in facilitating superconductivity. This interruption suggests that the LQD phase actively promotes superconductivity, rather than simply being a passive bystander. The implications extend beyond simply refining existing models of superconductivity. The energy scale of lattice dynamics, ranging from tens to hundreds of Kelvin, is comparable to the T c of high-temperature superconductors, meaning that thermal effects influencing nuclear quantum fluctuations cannot be ignored. The researchers emphasize that superconductivity should be viewed as a macroscopic quantum state of both electronic and lattice degrees of freedom. The discovery of this LQD phase represents a departure from conventional understanding, as quantum disorder, in this context, is distinct from the dynamically or spatially disordered local moments observed in other systems. While previous studies incorporated essential quantum corrections, they did not fully address the many-body nature of the interacting nuclei, leaving a gap in the understanding of structural phase transitions and their relationship to superconductivity. The recent emergence of nickel-based superconductors, coupled with enhanced structural characterization under pressure, provided a timely platform for validating this new picture of quantum lattice disorder and its role in facilitating superconductivity. This transition stems from a structural shift from a low-symmetry phase into the LQD phase, a finding supported by path-integral molecular dynamics (PIMD) used to accurately model the quantum behavior of the nuclei. The consistency of this alignment across different exchange-correlation functionals further strengthens the connection between the LQD phase and the superconducting mechanism. The location of the LQD phase’s boundary is not merely correlated with the superconducting dome’s peak T c ; it coincides with it, indicating that the quantum disorder actively contributes to, rather than simply accompanies, superconductivity.
